meta.title: AI tools across review stages
meta.snapshotQualification: RAISE 3 v4 p. 3 calls Table 2 a September 2026 snapshot; the p. 12 caption still says February 2026. This map identifies the exact document version rather than treating the table as a live product catalogue.
meta.licence: RAISE sources: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International; this guide is an independent adaptation.

recommendations.label: Acceptable for use
recommendations.description: Outputs may be used directly when their limitations and potential biases are acknowledged and addressed.

recommendations.label: Human verification required
recommendations.description: A human must carefully check outputs before use—typically the entire output—and correct them as needed. Fluent or plausible wording does not demonstrate accuracy.

recommendations.label: Requires validation within the review
recommendations.description: Test the intended task and workflow within this review against a task-specific threshold set in advance and an appropriate benchmark. The workflow must meet that standard; previous use elsewhere or convincing examples are insufficient.

recommendations.label: Exploratory and supplementary use
recommendations.description: Use outputs to develop ideas, with extensive human refinement before using them in a review, or to supplement established processes without replacing them.

recommendations.label: Not acceptable for use
recommendations.description: Outputs have serious limitations for the specified use and should not be relied upon.

functions.descriptionMd: ASySD identifies repeated bibliographic records in search results, allowing a review to retain a single record rather than screen the same publication repeatedly. Its developers provide both an R package and a web application.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes deduplication as comparing bibliographic fields against prescribed similarity criteria. For ASySD, the developer paper describes metadata cleaning, candidate matching, string comparisons and decision rules, rather than a generative model writing a decision. See the [ASySD development and evaluation paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10483700/).
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE identifies deduplication as a mature application and notes low false-positive rates for many validated tools. Its qualification matters: matching logic can be domain-specific, so assess suitability for the actual records and retain an audit trail of duplicate pairs where possible. This is a row-level justification, rather than an assurance of error-free ASySD performance in every review.
functions.officialUrlMd: [ASySD developer repository](https://github.com/camaradesuk/ASySD), which links its R package documentation and Shiny application.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; supporting discussion, pp. 5–6.

functions.descriptionMd: Support structured confidence assessment of findings from a qualitative evidence synthesis. CERQual is an assessment approach, not the name of a standalone AI program. The official site distinguishes the framework from iSoQ, the online platform that helps authors apply it.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Table 2 places GRADE-CERQual among template-based resources supporting established assessment frameworks. The bounded, structured application of criteria explains the rule-based grouping; it does not mean the framework autonomously reads all studies and determines confidence.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE explicitly preserves human certainty judgements. Interpretation: a structured template can organise and document those judgements without delegating them to an opaque generative system. The recommendation therefore concerns assistance with applying a framework, not automated adjudication of qualitative findings or a claim that CERQual itself is AI software.
functions.officialUrlMd: [GRADE-CERQual](https://www.cerqual.org/). The coordinating team's site separately links the [iSoQ application](https://isoq.epistemonikos.org/).
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18 (template support; humans retain certainty judgements). General certainty-assessment background, p. 9; product-specific details are attributed to the linked official resources.

functions.descriptionMd: Assist with assessing confidence in network meta-analysis findings. The official documentation describes a structured framework covering within-study bias, reporting bias, indirectness, imprecision, heterogeneity and incoherence, including a contribution matrix that shows how studies inform network estimates.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE groups it with tools that implement established certainty-assessment frameworks. Prespecified calculations and structured presentation support reviewers' assessments; this is distinct from asking an LLM to invent or independently deliver a final certainty rating.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE's stated boundary is that humans still make certainty judgements. Interpretation: CINeMA can make the inputs and assessment pathway more organised and inspectable, while reviewers remain responsible for evaluating concerns and the resulting confidence rating. The Table 2 entry is not a blanket endorsement of an unattended pipeline from raw studies to recommendations.
functions.officialUrlMd: [CINeMA](https://cinema.med.auth.gr/). The [University of Bern development repository](https://github.com/esm-ispm-unibe-ch/cinema) documents the application.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18 (template support; humans retain certainty judgements). General certainty-assessment background, p. 9; product-specific details are attributed to the linked official resources.

functions.descriptionMd: Obtain references cited by known relevant papers and papers that cite them, to discover potentially eligible studies missed by the main keyword search. The official implementation describes forward and backward retrieval using bibliographic citation data.
functions.whyCategoryMd: This function follows recorded citation relationships and sends requests through database software interfaces (APIs) according to a defined procedure. It retrieves linked records for reviewer consideration, rather than generating an account of which studies ought to exist or independently deciding eligibility.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE says citation chasing is useful where keyword indexing is weak. It also warns that results depend on the citation database's coverage and can favour older or heavily cited work. Interpretation: its value is as an additional search route with documented starting papers and data sources, while the reviewer still evaluates the retrieved evidence and documents the search.
functions.officialUrlMd: [citationchaser developer repository](https://github.com/nealhaddaway/citationchaser), linking the [web application named in RAISE](https://estech.shinyapps.io/citationchaser/).
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, pp. 13–14 (citation-chasing rationale and example-list continuation). General study-identification background, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: In RAISE's use, search results are checked against a reference set of articles to see which benchmark records were retrieved. CiteSource's documentation describes preserving search-source and search-string metadata while merging records, enabling comparisons of what different searches contribute.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The listed function concerns record matching, identifiers, deduplication and coverage counts. These operations make the relationship between a specified reference set and retrieved records inspectable; they are not a generative model's judgement that a search is adequate.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Table 2 describes the matching-based workflow but gives no separate CiteSource-specific rationale. Interpretation: it offers a transparent check of a concrete benchmark. Coverage is conditional on the benchmark's quality: retrieving every article in a small or biased reference set does not prove that a search retrieves all relevant literature. Reviewers must still judge the strategy and benchmark.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14 (query validation). The benchmark-quality limitation is editorial interpretation of the reference-set check.

functions.descriptionMd: Citation chasing, as classified in RAISE: use a known paper to find related literature beyond the original keyword results. Its official explanation is more precise than the broad row label: the visual connections reflect similarity based on co-citation (being cited together) and bibliographic coupling (sharing references), and the graph is not simply a tree of direct citations.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE assigns this search use to its rule-based row. Interpretation: citation relationships and a specified graph-similarity procedure offer an identifiable retrieval mechanism. This should not be expanded into a claim that every part of the current product is fixed-rule-only or that every displayed edge means one paper cites another.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE values discovery of studies missed by keywords but flags citation-index coverage and citation bias. A related-paper graph can support additional discovery; it does not demonstrate comprehensive retrieval or remove the need to screen candidates.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, pp. 13–14 (citation-chasing rationale and example-list continuation). General study-identification background, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: Quantitative analysis using dedicated meta-analysis applications. The official CRSU site describes R Shiny interfaces for statistical synthesis, visualisation and sensitivity analysis; the label denotes a suite rather than one algorithm.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes such applications as executing underlying R or Python calculations on effect estimates and summary statistics using user-defined parameters. Established statistical models perform the pooling; text generation is not the synthesis mechanism.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE requires documented, adjustable statistical parameters and reviewers who can choose appropriate analyses. It also stresses input-data quality. Interpretation: automating computation is acceptable when the reviewer remains responsible for the method and assumptions. The recommendation does not decide whether studies should be pooled or select an appropriate model on the user's behalf.
functions.officialUrlMd: [CRSU meta-analysis apps, University of Glasgow](https://www.gla.ac.uk/research/az/crsu/apps/). The verified official suite uses **CRSU**.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17; supporting discussion, pp. 8–9.

functions.descriptionMd: Duplicate removal from bibliographic search results. The developer describes a dedicated automated deduplication product. Only this Table 2 function is represented here.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE places this deduplication use in its rule-based category. The [published 2022 implementation](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-022-02045-9) describes preprocessing using natural language processing (NLP), metadata normalisation, similarity comparisons and expert-derived rules for identifying duplicates. This supports the specific matching function shown here; it is not a complete audit of every component in the current proprietary product.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE cites the maturity of validated deduplication approaches, while warning that domain-specific matching logic may not generalise. Interpretation: check the product's evidence and the input records' suitability, and retain transparent duplicate decisions where possible. RAISE's row does not substantiate vendor performance claims for every dataset.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; supporting discussion, pp. 5–6. The mechanism description is additionally supported by Borissov and colleagues’ 2022 methods paper, linked above.

functions.descriptionMd: Display a review's coded evidence as an interactive evidence-and-gap map. The official documentation describes exporting coded data from EPPI-Reviewer and configuring its presentation in EPPI-Mapper. The display helps readers inspect where evidence is concentrated or sparse.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Table 2 calls this “rule-based software.” Interpretation: the function maps supplied structured data into a configured visual arrangement. It does not independently judge the evidential meaning of a gap or generate a cross-study conclusion.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE 3 v4 explicitly describes visualisations of study characteristics, including evidence-and-gap maps. Interpretation: rendering reviewer-generated coding can be checked against its underlying data. Reviewers remain responsible for the coding, map dimensions, filters and interpretation; a visually empty cell does not by itself establish absence of relevant research.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17 (visual synthesis). The explanation of checkable rendering and the caution about empty cells are editorial interpretation of that row.

functions.descriptionMd: RAISE lists the platform as an interface for bringing bibliographic records into a review. The official help describes importing common reference formats and importing results of a PubMed search run from within EPPI-Reviewer.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The listed task is executing a specified retrieval/import procedure. RAISE expressly distinguishes individual functions within multipurpose review platforms: EPPI-Reviewer's classifiers or generative features should not be assigned the same category merely because they share a platform name.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE notes that programmatic retrieval is available through some platforms and that database access through software interfaces (APIs) is incomplete. Interpretation: a known query and documented import route can be incorporated transparently, but access, database coverage and successful transfer still need checking. Retrieving citation metadata does not imply obtaining all full texts or demonstrating the completeness of the review search.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; API-assisted retrieval discussion, p. 4; coverage and access limitations, p. 5.

functions.descriptionMd: The official project describes visualising datasets produced by systematic maps, including geographical evidence displays. It organises previously assembled and coded evidence for exploration and communication.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE labels this function “rule-based software.” Interpretation: structured records, geographic fields and user choices determine the resulting visual representation. The software's visualisation role is distinct from a model deciding what a body of evidence collectively proves.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE 3 v4 explicitly describes visualisations of study characteristics, including evidence-and-gap maps. Interpretation: rendering reviewer-generated coding can be checked against its underlying data. Reviewers remain responsible for the coding, map dimensions, filters and interpretation; a visually empty cell does not by itself establish absence of relevant research.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17 (visual synthesis). The explanation of checkable rendering and the caution about empty cells are editorial interpretation of that row.

functions.descriptionMd: Support the application and documentation of an established certainty-assessment framework. The official platform describes structured assessments, evidence tables and associated calculations.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE places the template-supported framework function in its rule-based row. Structured fields and predefined presentation/calculation procedures support a judgement process, rather than substituting an LLM's judgement for reviewers' assessments. Other current platform features do not alter the scope of this particular entry.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE's explicit condition is that humans still make certainty judgements. Interpretation: standardised recording can help users apply and report the framework consistently, but reviewers must assess the underlying evidence and justify their ratings. A well-completed template is not evidence that every substantive judgement is sound, and the recommendation does not endorse automated certainty assessment across all platform functions.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18 (template support; humans retain certainty judgements). General certainty-assessment background, p. 9; product-specific details are attributed to the linked official resources.

functions.descriptionMd: Quantitative analysis using a dedicated R meta-analysis package. The official package describes standard meta-analysis models and associated plots. RAISE uses the package as an example of software that performs specified statistical analysis on supplied data.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Here “rule-based” refers to running defined statistical procedures with chosen parameters. It is conventional statistical programming, rather than a generative model reading study prose and improvising a synthesis. The lower-case package name is retained to distinguish the software identity.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE requires statistical parameters to be documented and adjustable to analytical choices. Its narrative also requires sound inputs and sufficient analytical knowledge. Interpretation: reproducible computation can support a defensible synthesis, while the reviewer must still select effect measures and models, assess whether pooling is meaningful, and interpret heterogeneity and sensitivity analyses.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17; supporting discussion, pp. 8–9.

functions.descriptionMd: The developer's documentation describes R functions for effect-size calculation, fitting meta-analytic models, moderator/meta-regression analysis and plots. This entry represents RAISE's statistical-analysis use rather than every possible package operation.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The supplied data, model specification and statistical routines determine the calculations. RAISE's broad rule-based grouping encompasses this conventional software; it is not a claim that meta-analysis is generative AI or that the package independently develops an evidence-synthesis argument.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE requires transparent, adjustable statistical parameters and human analytical expertise. Interpretation: inspectable code and outputs support accountability, but cannot correct an inappropriate synthesis question or invalidly combined studies. Reviewers remain responsible for data preparation, dependence structures, assumptions, model choice and the meaning of results.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17; supporting discussion, pp. 8–9.

functions.descriptionMd: The platform can execute searches through supported database software interfaces (APIs) and import bibliographic search files; these are ways to bring records into a review workspace. These details are described in its official documentation.
functions.whyCategoryMd: This entry covers the defined search-execution and record-transfer function. The separately listed Smart Search feature has an agentic classification. That feature and other AI functions do not share the generic platform's rule-based citation-retrieval classification.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE says retrieval can be automated or carried out through a review platform, but API access is not universal. Interpretation: reviewers should document database, query, date and transfer route, check restrictions and verify that expected records were imported. The favourable category does not mean all databases are covered, that full text is always obtained, or that an automated search is inherently comprehensive.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; API-assisted retrieval discussion, p. 4; coverage and access limitations, p. 5.

functions.descriptionMd: Estimate the time and resources needed to conduct a review from user-supplied parameters. The estimate supports planning; it does not perform the review tasks.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE places this estimation tool in the rule-based class. The developer describes an algorithm combining expected evidence volumes and working speeds, with editable assumptions. This is a structured calculation, not an LLM independently planning or conducting the review.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE lists resource estimation as acceptable. Interpretation: reviewers can inspect and adapt the assumptions while retaining responsibility for the plan. Default estimates reflect their underlying contexts and should not be treated as a guaranteed completion time or as evidence that an under-resourced review is feasible.
functions.officialUrlMd: [PredicTER — official tool and methods](https://predicter.github.io/). The developer explains that default evidence volumes and working speeds came from environmental reviews and a survey of experienced reviewers, and can be tailored.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 12. The mechanism/default-context explanation is from the linked official tool page; the planning caveat is source-aligned interpretation.

functions.descriptionMd: The application analyses PubMed results and produces frequency tables, including words used in titles/abstracts and indexing information. Reviewers can use these patterns to identify candidate search terms.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Counting and tabulating terms from a specified set of records is a defined text-analysis operation. It provides observable information about that sample rather than generating unsupported terminology or deciding the final search strategy.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE treats term-frequency analysis as a useful complement to other search-development methods and specialist expertise. Interpretation: terms suggested by the initial result set can improve a search, but also inherit omissions and bias from that set. A PubMed-oriented tool cannot by itself resolve indexing differences in every database or prove adequate sensitivity.
functions.officialUrlMd: [PubReMiner, Amsterdam UMC/AMC](https://hgserver2.amc.nl/cgi-bin/miner/miner2.cgi), the application linked in RAISE.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 13; supporting discussion, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: Citation chasing within RAISE's broad search row: explore literature connected to known papers to identify additional candidates. The current official site describes interactive maps of papers, authors and concepts alongside an adaptive recommendation engine.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE places this function in its rule-based citation-chasing row. The developer documentation describes algorithms that learn from user activity, so the classification should not be read as a complete description of the current product's architecture. The category shown here applies to the function in RAISE's September 2026 v4 guidance.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE says citation-linked discovery can find studies missed by keyword searches, with limitations from citation-database coverage and bias toward older or frequently cited work. Interpretation: use it as a documented additional discovery route and screen the resulting candidates. Personalised recommendations are not proof that all relevant studies have been retrieved.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, pp. 13–14 (citation-chasing rationale and example-list continuation). General study-identification background, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: The developers describe finding overrepresented terms in a set of relevant references so that information specialists can incorporate them into Boolean searches (which combine terms using operators such as AND and OR). The application supports text analysis of free-text terms and controlled vocabulary (standardised indexing terms).
functions.whyCategoryMd: The listed operation applies explicit quantitative text-analysis procedures to a supplied reference set. It assists a reviewer in selecting candidate terms; it does not independently create and certify a complete systematic-review search.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE permits term-frequency support when combined with other search-development methods. Interpretation: its structured outputs can help expose relevant terminology, while expert judgement remains necessary to assess the sample, test the resulting search and adapt it to database indexing. The recommendation does not establish that any reference set yields an adequate final strategy.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 13; supporting discussion, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: Study selection using domain-specific population, intervention, comparison and outcome (PICO) dictionaries. Table 2 names Systematic Online Living Evidence Summaries (SOLES) parenthetically as an example where such dictionaries are used. The coloured cell refers to manually constructed regular-expression rules that identify study characteristics, particularly in full text; it does not represent every component of a SOLES workflow.
functions.whyCategoryMd: These dictionaries encode terms and matching patterns chosen by people, rather than learning a classifier from labelled examples. SOLES itself is a broader framework that may combine several technologies, not a single universal rule-based screening application.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE warns that handcrafted dictionaries cannot adapt to unfamiliar terminology. Interpretation: test whether the chosen rules correctly recognise the review's concepts and relevant language before relying on them, including the risk of missed studies. A dictionary useful in one domain is not automatically adequate in another.
functions.officialUrlMd: [CAMARADES SOLES project directory](https://camaradesuk.github.io/soles-projects/), linked by the team's [systematic-review wiki](https://camarades.de/wiki-content/11-tools.html).
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 15; supporting discussion, pp. 6–7.

functions.descriptionMd: RAISE names the overall TERA platform as an example of obtaining bibliographic records programmatically or through a review interface. This general platform entry is separate from the named TERA features listed in this map.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The specified function concerns carrying out a retrieval procedure and transferring records. The category does not describe the whole platform or imply that every named TERA feature has the same mechanism and recommendation.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE notes that not every database provides a software interface (API) for automated retrieval. Interpretation: a platform can reduce manual record handling when the underlying sources, queries and limits are known, but users still need to check coverage, successful transfer and provenance. This entry does not establish unrestricted database access, automatic full-text availability, or the completeness of a search.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; API-assisted retrieval discussion, p. 4; coverage and access limitations, p. 5.

functions.descriptionMd: Identify repeated records after combining results from different searches or databases, reducing redundant screening while retaining the evidence record.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE places Deduplicator in the row for metadata matching according to prescribed similarity criteria. This describes the deduplication function, rather than every function available elsewhere in TERA.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE describes deduplication as mature and notes low false-positive rates among validated tools, but warns that specialised matching logic may not generalise. Interpretation: use matching appropriate to the input records, consider the consequences of deleting a genuinely distinct report, and retain duplicate-pair evidence where available. The Table 2 recommendation is not a guarantee that every proposed duplicate can be accepted without attention to context.
functions.officialUrlMd: [TERA official tool/help directory](https://tera-tools.com/help/), which lists the named feature.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; supporting discussion, pp. 5–6.

functions.descriptionMd: Adapt an existing bibliographic search to the search syntax used by another database or platform. This concerns the command language used to express the strategy, rather than translating study text or automatically establishing that the strategy's concepts are suitable. RAISE 2 notes that syntax translators do not translate controlled vocabularies such as MeSH or CINAHL headings; these must be selected and checked separately.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE places the feature in its rule-based query-translation row. Interpretation: predefined conversions between search conventions can automate repetitive syntax changes. They do not remove the need to understand database-specific indexing and search behaviour.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE identifies changing database interfaces, uneven maintenance and validation, and limited specialist-database coverage as vulnerabilities. Reviewers should check the complete translated query, correct unsupported or outdated syntax, and establish that the intended concepts and retrieval behaviour are preserved. This stronger verification requirement is why Polyglot differs from the generally acceptable rule-based search functions around it.
functions.officialUrlMd: [TERA Polyglot](https://tera-tools.com/polyglot), the application linked in RAISE, and the [official help directory](https://tera-tools.com/help/).
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; supporting discussion, pp. 4–5. RAISE 2 v4 (25 August 2026), p. 17 describes the controlled-vocabulary limitation.

functions.descriptionMd: Help structure and draft the review’s methods section using supplied information and a template. RAISE Table 2 places this structured-reporting function under “Text Generation”; this map presents it under “Writing a manuscript”. It does not imply autonomous interpretation of review results.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes a template tool: predefined structure supports the report, rather than a general-purpose LLM generating substantive conclusions from the evidence. Interpretation: standardised fields and text scaffolding can organise information supplied by the review team.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE states the structured-reporting role but provides little additional justification in the row. Interpretation: an inspectable template can assist reporting while users supply the actual methods and findings. Reviewers must ensure that the resulting text accurately describes their review; acceptance of templating does not authorise invented methods, synthesis or conclusions.
functions.officialUrlMd: [TERA official tool/help directory](https://tera-tools.com/help/), which lists the named feature. A [researcher’s TERA training presentation](https://www.ebm-netzwerk.de/de/medien/pdf/ebm2025-k-02-02-thomas.pdf) identifies methods-section drafting as the specific role.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18 (rule-based structured reporting). The methods-section specificity comes from the separately linked TERA training presentation; the accountability caveat is editorial interpretation.

functions.descriptionMd: RAISE describes checking search results against a reference set to establish coverage, with matching or deduplication algorithms and unique identifiers helping identify the relevant overlaps.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The mapped function compares explicit records and counts or identifies matches. Interpretation: those prescribed comparisons make the benchmark check reproducible, rather than relying on a model's unobservable opinion that a query looks adequate.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Table 2 supplies the operational description but no separate product-specific justification. Interpretation: a reference-set comparison provides concrete evidence about a query's behaviour. It is limited by the benchmark: passing the check does not establish complete retrieval outside that set. Information specialists still need to assess concepts, database syntax and whether refinements discard genuinely relevant studies.
functions.officialUrlMd: [TERA official tool/help directory](https://tera-tools.com/help/), which lists the named feature.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14 (query validation). The benchmark-quality limitation is editorial interpretation of the reference-set check.

functions.descriptionMd: Search strategy development through term-frequency analysis. Reviewers use words recurring in preliminary search results to identify candidate terminology that may expand or refine the strategy.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes explicit counting of keywords and/or controlled-vocabulary terms. The useful output is a summary of language present in the supplied records, rather than a generated assertion about all terminology relevant to the research question.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE says frequency tools should be combined with other development methods and information-specialist expertise. Interpretation: a frequent term may be useful, while a rare but essential synonym may be absent. The initial sample, database indexing and reviewer decisions therefore remain important; frequency alone should not determine which terms enter the final search.
functions.officialUrlMd: [TERA WordFreq](https://tera-tools.com/word-freq), the application linked in RAISE. The feature is also listed in the [official help directory](https://tera-tools.com/help/).
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 13; supporting discussion, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: The application retrieves metadata for supplied PubMed identifiers and arranges indexing terms in a comparison grid. The official help explains that reviewers can inspect Medical Subject Headings (MeSH), variants and indexing differences to understand why known articles were retrieved or missed.
functions.whyCategoryMd: This is a specified retrieval, sorting and display procedure applied to existing bibliographic metadata. RAISE groups it with keyword/controlled-vocabulary analysis; it helps the searcher see term patterns rather than independently reasoning that a complete strategy has been achieved.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE treats these tools as complements to other search-development approaches. Interpretation: the grid makes indexing evidence easier to inspect, but reviewers must choose appropriate articles, assess useful terms and adapt the strategy for each database. MeSH-based inspection does not establish that indexing is consistent or that concepts outside the sample have been covered.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 13; supporting discussion, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: Cluster supplied literature into topics to help reviewers identify themes and areas of interest while developing a protocol.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE assigns this function to **Unsupervised** learning rather than supervised classification. It discovers structure in the supplied text without needing reviewers to label examples as eligible or ineligible. Clustering and labelling groups is distinct from deciding which studies belong in a review or generating an evidence-based answer.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE 3 v4 explicitly lists topic exploration during protocol development as acceptable. Clusters can help orient the review team, which remains responsible for question choice, protocol decisions and subsequent comprehensive searching; this is not validation of every cluster or an automated evidence synthesis.
functions.officialUrlMd: [Carrot2 search-results clustering](https://search.carrot2.org/). [Developer documentation/source](https://github.com/carrot2/carrot2) confirms that it groups related documents and labels the groups. The search interface requires JavaScript.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 12; technology classes, p. 3. RAISE 2 v4 (25 August 2026), p. 6 explains unsupervised learning and topic modelling.

functions.descriptionMd: Groups search results or other supplied documents into topic clusters, helping a reviewer recognise themes, terminology and possible areas of interest.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE assigns this function to **Unsupervised** learning rather than supervised classification. It discovers structure in the supplied text without needing reviewers to label examples as eligible or ineligible. Clustering and labelling groups is distinct from deciding which studies belong in a review or generating an evidence-based answer.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: The table explicitly describes rapid topic exploration. **Interpretation:** using clusters to orient the researcher leaves formal search design and eligibility decisions with the team. It does not certify exhaustive retrieval, valid thematic synthesis, or the quality of every cluster. The general acceptable category still requires limitations and potential biases to be accounted for. This recommendation applies to the exploratory function described above.

functions.descriptionMd: Uses human screening decisions to rank remaining citations. In this workflow the review team stops before every record has been manually screened, adding a stopping decision to prioritisation.
functions.aiCategoryMd: **Supervised prioritised screening algorithms where early stopping is used**
functions.whyCategoryMd: Supervised algorithms learn relevance from reviewer-labelled records and update the screening order. Early stopping adds a decision to leave some records unread; that is distinct from merely changing their order.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE requires within-review validation when screening stops early. The team must assess the configured algorithm and stopping procedure against prespecified requirements for sensitivity (the proportion of all relevant records identified), using suitable review records. A high yield near the start or a run of irrelevant records does not establish that the unscreened remainder contains no relevant studies. Time savings may be small when maximum sensitivity is required.

Classification and prioritised screening are distinct methodological roles; listing them is not a separate product-wide endorsement of each feature.

The narrative says evaluations commonly use domain-specific datasets under controlled conditions, and new review applications need context-specific evaluation. **Interpretation:** identifying a plausible entity is insufficient if the wrong exposure, group or experiment is linked to it; validation should cover the intended extraction workflow.

functions.descriptionMd: Builds or applies a model that assigns records a class or relevance score. Bespoke models can learn from examples manually assigned to two classes; a team then chooses how the scores affect its review.
functions.whyCategoryMd: These models learn a mapping from labelled text to a prediction. Unlike prioritised screening, this entry concerns the prediction model itself, rather than the ongoing ordering of a screening queue.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: **Explicit rationale:** appropriate training and validation data determine performance; complex concepts can require more varied examples, and training on titles and abstracts does not automatically transfer to other material. RAISE further warns that a well-developed classifier can be unsuitable outside its validated record type or domain. This row does not confer one shared performance claim on all EPPI-Reviewer models, including its separately evaluated pre-built classifiers.

This is a platform capability, not a separate standalone product.

functions.descriptionMd: Identifies reporting of items such as random allocation, blinded outcome assessment, animal exclusions, conflicts of interest and animal-welfare compliance. Reporting a safeguard does not establish low overall risk of bias.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Trained neural models predict outputs for individual reporting items; the repository lists convolutional neural networks (CNNs), attention-based models, hierarchical attention networks (HANs) and BERT approaches. A BERT-based classifier is not thereby a generative conversational LLM. RAISE places this function under **Reporting quality**, although the repository uses risk-of-bias terminology.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: **Explicit rationale:** performance depends heavily on the training corpus and domain. The critical-appraisal narrative also explains the difficulty of defining reliable reference judgements. **Interpretation:** validate the actual reporting items and study domain before using predictions in a review, and avoid upgrading detection of relevant sentences into an independently established bias judgement.
functions.officialUrlMd: [RAISE-linked Pre-ROB repository](https://github.com/camaradesuk/pre-rob). It describes neural models that predict reporting scores and retrieve sentences for preclinical risk-of-bias-related items.

functions.descriptionMd: Proposes assessments for selected domains of the original Cochrane risk-of-bias (RoB 1) framework and highlights supporting text to assist human appraisal. This conventional RobotReviewer function is not a validated RoB 2 assessment.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE assigns **Supervised machine learning**: trained models make task-specific predictions from trial reports. This entry concerns that appraisal function, not autonomous synthesis or all possible versions/features.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: **Explicit rationale:** training corpus and domain strongly affect performance; critical appraisal is judgement-dependent and reference assessors can disagree. The reported prior evaluation in the narrative does not establish universal accuracy. **Interpretation:** use a suitable independent assessment procedure to evaluate the outputs for the intended review and appraisal framework. The appraisal instrument matters: evidence for original RoB 1 domains does not establish validity for RoB 2 or another instrument. Cochrane’s risk-of-bias workshop explicitly distinguishes these comparisons.

functions.descriptionMd: Annotates population, intervention, comparator and outcome information in trial PDFs.

functions.whyRecommendationMd: **Explicit rationale:** domain and training corpora affect extraction performance. **Interpretation:** good performance on one task does not establish accuracy on another; assess extraction for the variables and reports actually used.

functions.functionName: Risk of bias assessment in the RAISE table
functions.descriptionMd: Provides signals relevant to appraisal, including whether methods report randomisation, blinding, power analysis or other safeguards. **Scope qualification:** the current product describes reporting/integrity checks; it explicitly does not claim to determine whether the science is correct. Do not describe its score as a complete independent risk-of-bias assessment.
functions.whyCategoryMd: This is RAISE's assignment. The developer describes trained detection algorithms, but the material checked does not establish a complete training design for every current component. This is not evidence that all its features use one model.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: **Explicit rationale:** appraisal performance depends strongly on training corpus and domain. **Interpretation:** validation must also ask whether the product's narrower reporting outputs answer the review's actual bias-assessment question. A detected statement about randomisation does not by itself establish adequate randomisation.
functions.officialUrlMd: [SciScore](https://sciscore.com/). The developer describes automated methods-reporting, rigour and resource-identifier checks, with editors and reviewers retaining scientific judgement.

functions.descriptionMd: Searches neuroscience animal-study publications for experimental characteristics and reporting of safeguards such as randomisation or blinding, producing structured reporting indicators.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE lists STEED as **Supervised machine learning**; this map retains that assignment. **Qualification:** its [published methods](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0311358) and linked code describe rule-based text matching (regular expressions), rather than a learned classifier.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: **Explicit rationale for the table row:** performance depends on the training data and review context. The neighbouring rule-based reporting-quality row also requires local validation. **Interpretation:** detecting a matching phrase is sensitive to wording and article context, and establishes reporting rather than actual experimental conduct. Neither classification justifies treating its output as a definitive appraisal without relevant validation.

functions.descriptionMd: Combines outputs in a pipeline to propose evidence-quality ratings. It is research software for partial automation, not a statement that contextual GRADE judgement has been solved. The repository requires RobotReviewer integration.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes supervised machine-learning tools linked in a pipeline; this map retains that assignment. **Qualification:** URSE combines RobotReviewer’s learned components with [fixed extraction and scoring rules](https://github.com/alisson-mfc/urse/blob/main/server/controllers/comparators.py). It is a hybrid system, rather than a single trained classifier that assigns the final certainty rating.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: **RAISE narrative:** URSE is described as proof-of-concept; such tools cannot be applied independently without stringent manual checking, which limits efficiency gains. **Separate evaluation context:** Its linked proof-of-concept evaluation concerns an adapted GRADE workflow; the authors themselves withhold support for full automation. **Interpretation:** URSE may inform exploration or add a checked supplementary output while established human certainty assessment remains in place. This is the exploratory and supplementary category, rather than the within-review-validation category used for many classifier uses.
functions.officialUrlMd: [URSE author repository](https://github.com/alisson-mfc/urse). The [RAISE-cited proof-of-concept article](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40194821/) identifies that repository and describes an adaptation of GRADE for reviews with meta-analyses of randomised trials.

functions.whyRecommendationMd: Fluent text does not establish that studies are compatible, transformations are correct, or weighting and treatment of uncertainty and heterogeneity are appropriate. This restriction differs from checked code assistance.

functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 15; supporting discussion, pp. 6–7.

functions.descriptionMd: Generate proposed appraisal judgements from study reports and explicit instructions.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model generates interpretive assessments rather than checking only fixed reporting features.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Incomplete or ambiguous reports can lead to invented or overconfident judgements. Evaluate performance in the review’s context; careful prompting and human verification remain necessary and do not resolve genuinely missing evidence.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 16; supporting discussion, p. 8.

functions.descriptionMd: Extract defined textual characteristics, such as populations, interventions, exposures, comparators and outcomes.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model generates field entries from instructions and source text, rather than solely using dictionaries.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Prompts, fields and documents affect performance. Evaluate the complete local procedure for omissions and invented content; a completed table is not proof of accuracy.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 16; supporting discussion, p. 7.

functions.descriptionMd: Extract numerical data, retaining the corresponding outcome and study group.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model generates requested field values by interpreting documents, rather than importing structured data.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Values may be wrong, missing or invented. Assess numerical accuracy and consequences of error in the intended workflow, including human checking, before using the data for analysis.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17; supporting discussion, p. 7.

functions.descriptionMd: Draft analysis scripts or suggest corrections to existing code.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model generates source code; the subsequent execution is a separate computational step.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Someone with coding and analytical knowledge must check the intended operation and results. Code that runs may still perform an inappropriate analysis. Applying RAISE’s general restriction, asking this same chatbot to generate the formal cross-study findings instead would fall under **Not acceptable for use**. This applies the general principle; Table 2 does not list this chatbot separately for that use.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17; supporting discussion, pp. 8–9.

functions.descriptionMd: Generate provisional manuscript prose or a reporting outline from supplied instructions and material.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model composes text rather than populating only a fixed template.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: The output is a starting point requiring extensive human refinement. Drafting does not authorise the underlying synthesis: generated interpretations across studies risk unsupported or incorrect conclusions.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18; supporting discussion, p. 10.

functions.descriptionMd: Shorten, simplify or rephrase existing text, or turn supplied bullets into paragraphs.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model generates alternative wording; the intended task is language revision.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Inspect the entire revision for changes to scientific meaning, numbers and qualifications. Fluency does not guarantee fidelity, and an omitted condition may materially alter what the manuscript claims.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18 (revisions); Table 1, p. 11 (human verification normally requires reading the entirety of the output). Related text-generation background, p. 10.

functions.descriptionMd: Re-express the team’s human-drafted overall review findings for a wider audience.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model generates accessible wording from an existing synthesis, rather than determining its findings.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Check all output for changes in meaning and unsupported claims, and ensure uncertainty is retained. This concerns communicating established conclusions, not accepting an automatically generated synthesis of separate studies.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18; supporting discussion, p. 10.

functions.descriptionMd: Ask Google AI Mode to generate the overall conclusion across quantitative studies in place of conducting the required synthesis analysis.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model produces the cross-study account, even if agents also retrieve sources.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Fluent text does not establish that studies are compatible, transformations are correct, or weighting and treatment of uncertainty and heterogeneity are appropriate. This restriction differs from checked code assistance.
functions.officialUrlMd:
[https://search.google/ways-to-search/ai-mode/](https://search.google/ways-to-search/ai-mode/)

[Google describes](https://search.google/ways-to-search/ai-mode/) AI-generated answers with web links and follow-up questions. In these two Table 2 rows, the relevant output is the generated cross-study conclusion, so RAISE's literal class is **Generative LLMs**, even if the current search service also orchestrates retrieval. This entry is not a blanket judgement about ordinary web searching.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17; supporting discussion, pp. 8–9.

functions.descriptionMd: Ask Google AI Mode to supply an integrated substantive conclusion across studies, rather than assisting the researcher’s qualitative analysis.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model produces the cross-study account, even if agents also retrieve sources.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: An apparently coherent narrative is not evidence of defensible selection, reconciliation and interpretation. This restriction differs from researcher-led assistance with summaries, codes or themes that requires validation within the review.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17; supporting discussion, p. 9.

functions.descriptionMd: Translate titles, abstracts or relevant report passages so a human reviewer can assess eligibility. Google Translate supplies a language-access aid; it does not make the inclusion decision.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE's exact mixed-technology label is retained. Placement in the LLM column group is an explicit display exception, not a claim that every Google Translate language, mode or historical implementation uses a generative LLM. Google's later feature descriptions do not establish which model was used in older evaluations.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Table 2 explicitly requires human verification for translation of non-English studies. Applying that one translation recommendation to this stage is a derived association, not a separately validated screening recommendation. Cochrane guidance supports translation-assisted eligibility assessment. Ambiguous machine-translated wording should prompt clarification rather than a confident exclusion; verification concerns source-language meaning, not just fluent English.
functions.officialUrlMd: [Google Translate](https://translate.google.com/). RAISE's cited empirical sources include [Balk et al. (2013)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/2046-4053-2-97) and [Jackson et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.7326/M19-0891); historical evaluations do not establish current performance across all modes and languages.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18; supporting discussion, p. 10. Stage placement is an editorial application of the single machine-translation row, not an additional stage-specific RAISE rating. Additional contextual source: [Cochrane Handbook §4.4.5](https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-04#section-4-4-5) and [EPOC guidance](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/16094069211061950).

functions.descriptionMd: Translate methods or reporting passages needed by a human applying an appropriate appraisal or risk-of-bias method. The translated text is an input to that judgement, not an automated quality assessment.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE's exact mixed-technology label is retained. Placement in the LLM column group is an explicit display exception, not a claim that every Google Translate language, mode or historical implementation uses a generative LLM. Google's later feature descriptions do not establish which model was used in older evaluations.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Human verification required is RAISE's explicit translation recommendation; its application to this appraisal context is derived. An apparently absent or unclear safeguard may reflect a translation error. Check methodological wording that could affect the assessment against a reliable interpretation of the original text before treating an apparent shortcoming as a study limitation. No direct validation of Google Translate's ability to judge bias is claimed.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18; supporting discussion, p. 10. Stage placement is an editorial application of the single machine-translation row, not an additional stage-specific RAISE rating. Additional contextual source: [Cochrane Handbook §5.3.2](https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-05#section-5-3-2) distinguishes collecting methodological information from assessing it.

functions.functionName: Translation to support human data extraction
functions.descriptionMd: Translate report passages from which humans extract study characteristics, outcomes or results. Translation does not itself populate and validate a structured extraction form.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE's exact mixed-technology label is retained. Placement in the LLM column group is an explicit display exception, not a claim that every Google Translate language, mode or historical implementation uses a generative LLM. Google's later feature descriptions do not establish which model was used in older evaluations.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE explicitly requires verification of translation outputs; using that recommendation in this extraction context is a derived stage association. Its cited extraction research reports material accuracy limitations, with outcomes and results more problematic than simpler information on study design or interventions. Check outcome identities, groups, time points, denominators, units and statistical quantities against a reliable interpretation of the original text. Older language-specific evaluations do not guarantee current extraction or final-review accuracy.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18; supporting discussion, p. 10. Stage placement is an editorial application of the single machine-translation row, not an additional stage-specific RAISE rating. Additional contextual source: [Balk et al. (2013)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/2046-4053-2-97). The stage association is derived from the translation function.

functions.functionName: Translation of inputs to human synthesis
functions.descriptionMd: Make source findings and contextual passages accessible to the human synthesis team. Verified translated information can inform the chosen quantitative or qualitative method; the translator does not pool effects, establish themes or decide the conclusion across studies.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE's exact mixed-technology label is retained. Placement in the LLM column group is an explicit display exception, not a claim that every Google Translate language, mode or historical implementation uses a generative LLM. Google's later feature descriptions do not establish which model was used in older evaluations.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE's verification requirement applies to translation; its placement in this later review stage is this map’s interpretation. Numerical meaning and qualitative or cultural context require particular care. A readable translation does not establish that studies are compatible, analytical inputs are correct or interpretation is valid. This supporting use must not be read as permission for machine-generated cross-study synthesis, which RAISE treats separately.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18; supporting discussion, p. 10. Stage placement is an editorial application of the single machine-translation row, not an additional stage-specific RAISE rating. Additional contextual source: [Cochrane Handbook §21.11](https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-21#section-21-11).

functions.functionName: Translation of inputs to human certainty judgement
functions.descriptionMd: Provide checked translations of study information or explanations used by humans applying GRADE or CERQual. This may reuse passages translated earlier in the review rather than introduce a separate translation operation; Google Translate does not rate certainty.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE's exact mixed-technology label is retained. Placement in the LLM column group is an explicit display exception, not a claim that every Google Translate language, mode or historical implementation uses a generative LLM. Google's later feature descriptions do not establish which model was used in older evaluations.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: The explicit translation recommendation remains Human verification required, but this is the most indirect of the five derived stage associations. No direct performance evidence for certainty judgement is asserted. Errors in translated outcomes, methods or context can propagate into the assessment, so verify the source meaning and retain human judgement. Access through translation is not itself evidence that a GRADE or CERQual conclusion is valid.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18; supporting discussion, p. 10. Stage placement is an editorial application of the single machine-translation row, not an additional stage-specific RAISE rating. Additional contextual source: [Cochrane Handbook §21.12](https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-21#section-21-12).

functions.descriptionMd: Use GenAI assistance in MAXQDA to propose summaries, codes, subcodes or themes for researcher assessment.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model produces interpretive suggestions; ordinary manual coding is not the mapped AI function.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE lists assistance with summaries, codes, subcodes and themes, subject to within-review validation because performance depends on prompts and the analytical context. Researchers must check and take responsibility for the suggestions; generated codes are not established review findings. The narrative also warns that generated summaries can reproduce the original authors’ perspective or spin. The table does not establish that every workflow generating themes across studies is acceptable, or fully define the boundary with the cross-study synthesis it advises against automating. Do not accept generated text as the review’s cross-study findings.
functions.officialUrlMd:
[https://www.maxqda.com/](https://www.maxqda.com/)

The mapped component is **GenAI assistance within MAXQDA**, not its complete qualitative-analysis environment. [Official AI Assist guidance](https://help.maxqda.com/en/support/solutions/articles/80001135283-what-is-maxqda-ai-assist-) describes summaries and suggestions for codes or subcodes; [coding guidance](https://www.maxqda.com/help/ai-assist/ai-coding/coding-documents) explicitly asks researchers to review and refine suggestions. These pages clarify the component, rather than independently validating its use in a review.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17; qualitative-analysis discussion, p. 9; broader limitations, pp. 10–11.

functions.descriptionMd: Iteratively turn a question into candidate search strategies using internal and user feedback.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Agentic AI coordinates a sequence of search-development steps rather than generating one static response.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Retain specialist input to develop and check searches rather than replacing established search methods. The row gives little specific evaluation detail; the narrative warns against substituting generated strategies. Official documentation describes a PubMed-focused feature.
functions.officialUrlMd:
[https://about.nested-knowledge.com/docs/smart-search/](https://about.nested-knowledge.com/docs/smart-search/)

This is the named Smart Search feature, not all of Nested Knowledge. Its [official documentation](https://about.nested-knowledge.com/docs/smart-search/) describes refining a question through dialogue, generating candidate PubMed queries, and allowing users to inspect and finalise them. Vendor-reported validation is separate evidence and does not replace the category assigned in RAISE's dated table.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 13; supporting discussion, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: Use Undermind to become familiar with a topic and identify terminology and candidate papers.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Agentic AI develops, refines and performs searches from a natural-language request.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE 3 v4 limits agentic scoping to exploratory and supplementary use. Search choices and available data sources constrain the results, and users need to guide the agent. It may help early familiarisation but should not be relied on for formal evidence retrieval.
functions.officialUrlMd:
[https://www.undermind.ai/](https://www.undermind.ai/)

RAISE names Undermind for agentic exploration and supplementary retrieval. Its [official site](https://www.undermind.ai/) describes literature-search assistance and iterative research interaction. The live page's performance claims concern its own current benchmarks; they do not replace RAISE's September 2026 v4 evidence-synthesis recommendations or establish that a particular review has retrieved every eligible study.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 13; supporting discussion, p. 5.

functions.descriptionMd: Use Undermind to identify additional candidate studies alongside conventional searching.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Agentic AI selects and performs retrieval actions, rather than only generating prose.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE considers these systems insufficiently sensitive to replace established strategies or retrieval sources. Human input and verification remain necessary; useful extra papers do not demonstrate complete coverage.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; supporting discussion, p. 5.

functions.descriptionMd: Suggest axes or points on a figure to recover numerical values, with human correction.
functions.whyCategoryMd: “Generative LLMs” is RAISE’s assignment to the AI-feature row; the current model architecture is not independently confirmed here.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Clearly defined figures may permit useful assistance, but humans must inspect axes, points and values. Extraction from more complex images remains a research question.
functions.officialUrlMd:
[https://automeris.io/](https://automeris.io/)

RAISE's name refers specifically to the AI-assisted component of **WebPlotDigitizer**, not all digitisation algorithms. The [official documentation](https://automeris.io/docs/) describes computer vision combined with manual inputs; the [official repository](https://github.com/automeris-io/WebPlotDigitizer/blob/master/README.md) distinguishes its closed AI Assist component. These public descriptions do not establish that every current extraction algorithm is an LLM. The displayed category is RAISE's assignment, not an independent architecture audit.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17 (image extraction, human correction and oversight, and the limitation concerning complex images).

functions.functionName: Interacting with evidence synthesis data using a chatbot
functions.descriptionMd: Ask questions about existing evidence-synthesis data or documents, such as an evidence map. RAISE treats this interaction separately from the review stages.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE treats **chatbot interaction** as a mode of LLM use. This recommendation concerns that feature, not all InfraNodus network-analysis functions. Gaps in a text network do not establish gaps in the research evidence.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Answers can be inaccurate, incomplete or stray beyond the supplied data, raising concerns about accuracy, safety and bias. Check the underlying records; do not treat generated answers as established synthesis findings.
functions.officialUrlMd: [InfraNodus — official product](https://infranodus.com/) describes its text-exploration and knowledge-graph features.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 19; modes of use, p. 3. RAISE 2 v4 (25 August 2026), pp. 6–8.
